explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says the king "prepared a wedding banquet for his son" (Matthew 22:2). The whole feast is in honor of the son, so this is no ordinary dinner. When somebody throws a party for their own child, you know the oven has been working overtime.

A daughter makes sense for a wedding, but that's not what Jesus says. He says the king "prepared a wedding banquet for his son" (Matthew 22:2). The son is the one being honored here. It's an easy one to swap, since weddings have a lot of details to keep straight.

The servants in this parable are busy, but they're not the guests of honor. They're the ones sent out with the invitations (Matthew 22:3). The banquet is for the king's son: "The kingdom of heaven is like a king who prepared a wedding banquet for his son." (Matthew 22:2) The servants are the delivery crew, and honestly I respect the delivery crew.

Yes, baker. The king sends his servants to call those he had invited, "but they refused to come." (Matthew 22:3) Read that slowly. The invitation came from the king himself, and they said no. I have been shoved in a junk drawer, friend, and even I would show up for THAT party.

Not quite, baker. The text says the king sent his servants to call those he had invited, "but they refused to come." (Matthew 22:3) So the guests said no, and nobody was running to the door. The invitation was real, and the answer was no.

explanations.answer: Ignore him and go off to work
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. They "paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business." (Matthew 22:5) The king says everything is ready, and they walk off to their own stuff. I know that feeling, because I've kept a batch waiting while I finished one more little task, but I never did it to a KING.

explanations.answer: Ask him to pick a later date
explanations.explanation: That would at least be polite, but the text doesn't say it. These guests "paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business." (Matthew 22:5) Nobody asks for a new date. They just walk off to their own work.

Gifts would be a nice gesture, but nobody in the parable sends any. The text says they "paid no attention and went away, one to his field, another to his business." (Matthew 22:5) They turned away and went about their day. A card and a fruit basket doesn't show up anywhere in the story.

Yes, baker. "The king was enraged, and he sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city." (Matthew 22:7) This part is heavy, because the servants were killed in the verse before. The king's anger is the response to that.

Yes, baker. The king sends troops "to destroy those murderers and burn their city." (Matthew 22:7) It's a hard verse. The text says the king was enraged, and it comes right after his servants were killed.

The servants were the ones who got mistreated and killed (Matthew 22:6), so they're not the ones sent out here. The text says the king "sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city." (Matthew 22:7) The troops are a different group from the servants. It's heavy stuff, so it helps to keep who is who straight.

A field is where one of the guests ran off to (Matthew 22:5), so it's easy to see why it came to mind. But the king doesn't burn a field. He sent his troops "to destroy those murderers and burn their city." (Matthew 22:7) This is a heavy verse, so the words matter.

There are no ships anywhere in this parable, baker. The king "sent his troops to destroy those murderers and burn their city." (Matthew 22:7) So the answer is troops and city. Ships would be a whole different story, and a much more soggy one.

That's it, baker. The king says, "Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find." (Matthew 22:9) A crossroads is where roads meet and all kinds of people pass through. The servants are sent right where the foot traffic is.

The temple is where Jesus is teaching (Matthew 21:23), so it's a fair guess. But inside the parable, the king says, "Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find." (Matthew 22:9) The servants head out to the crossroads. That's a long way from the temple.

The palace is where the banquet is, so I see the thinking. But the king sends his servants out of it, not to it. He says, "Go therefore to the crossroads and invite to the banquet as many as you can find." (Matthew 22:9) A palace invitation wouldn't have reached anybody walking by.

Close, baker, but the king says nothing about important people. He tells the servants, "invite to the banquet as many as you can find." (Matthew 22:9) No list of titles, and nobody gets checked at the door for importance. The invitation just goes wide.
Yes, baker. The king says, "invite to the banquet as many as you can find." (Matthew 22:9) He doesn't say to pick out the important ones. The goal is a full hall, and anyone the servants find counts.

Yes, baker. The servants gathered "everyone they could find, both evil and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests." (Matthew 22:10) Notice that it says everyone. The hall fills up, and the invitation reaches far past the first guests.

That would be a smaller crowd, but it's not what the text says. The servants gathered "everyone they could find, both evil and good." (Matthew 22:10) Both kinds are in that hall. The word is everyone.

The text never says the guests were poor. It says the servants gathered "everyone they could find, both evil and good, and the wedding hall was filled with guests." (Matthew 22:10) The only two groups named are evil and good. I'd rather stick to what Jesus actually says.

explanations.answer: He isn't dressed in wedding clothes
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. "When the king came in to see the guests, he spotted a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes." (Matthew 22:11) Out of a whole hall, the king sees this one thing. The text doesn't tell us why the man didn't have them, and I won't guess.

explanations.answer: He came in without being invited
explanations.explanation: It's a smart guess, since the invitations went out wide. But the text doesn't say the man came uninvited. It says the king "spotted a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes." (Matthew 22:11) The clothes are what the king notices.

explanations.answer: He's sitting in the king's own seat
explanations.explanation: Now that would be a plot twist, baker. But Jesus doesn't say anything about a seat. The king "spotted a man who was not dressed in wedding clothes." (Matthew 22:11) The clothes are the whole detail.
Yes, baker. The king asks, "how did you get in here without wedding clothes?" and "the man was speechless." (Matthew 22:12) He has nothing to say. I think that's a very quiet moment in that hall.
The text doesn't say the man was sorry. After the king asks his question, "the man was speechless." (Matthew 22:12) He says nothing at all. So there's no apology and no excuse in the verse.

The man doesn't snap back, baker. When the king asks, "how did you get in here without wedding clothes?" the text says "the man was speechless." (Matthew 22:12) No words, angry or otherwise. I think that silence says a lot.

Not quite, baker. Jesus ends with this: "For many are called, but few are chosen." (Matthew 22:14) Many, and then few. If everyone called were also chosen, those two numbers would match, and they don't.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, "For many are called, but few are chosen." (Matthew 22:14) The two groups are not the same size. Many are called, and few are chosen.
